turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Hale, in you come. I've done your observations — blood pressure was 152 over 88, and your pulse was 76.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): 152 over 88, is that going to cause a stroke? I feel absolutely fine. I don't know why Jean's brought me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Because you keep asking the same— sorry, Doctor. He repeats himself, he's forgotten appointments, and last Tuesday he got lost on the way back from the paper shop.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll get there. I'm Dr Shah. Mr Hale, how old are you, just so I'm straight?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-eight. But is that blood pressure an emergency? That's the only thing actually wrong with me.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's higher than we'd like, not an emergency sitting here. Mrs Hale, when did you first notice him repeating questions?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): She's been on about the boiler man. He never turned up. That's the real argument, not my memory.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Arthur, the boiler was three weeks ago. The questions started in the autumn — September, I think, or just before. Three or four times in an hour, the same thing.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not do that. Once is enough for any question. She's building it up because she worries.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): I've heard you, Mr Hale. I still need the Tuesday story. What happened after the paper shop?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing happened. There were roadworks on the high street, so I went round the park. I was not lost.

[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was out nearly two hours. Mrs Kent from number twelve found him by the station, which is the opposite direction, and he couldn't say which bus would get him home.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mr Hale, do you remember being at the station?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I remember her talking. She always talks. I knew perfectly well where I was, so if I was lost, why did I... no, I wasn't.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have any appointments been missed?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The left knee, on the stairs, that's been a nuisance for a couple of years. Is that the sort of thing you meant?
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): I meant appointments — dentist, hospital, that kind of missed. We'll come to the knee in a minute. Mrs Hale?

[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dentist last month. It was written on the kitchen calendar and he still didn't go. The optician in January as well — I had to ring and apologise after he simply didn't arrive.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I knew the dentist was there. I chose not to sit in the chair. Choosing is not forgetting, so can we please—
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He told me the night before that the next day was clear. Nothing in it. You can't choose not to go to something you don't remember.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Two accounts, and I can't pick a winner in ten minutes. I'm not going to try. Any falls lately, any weakness on one side, or trouble getting words out?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No falls. Words are fine, you're listening to them. How long is this appointment? I thought I had— actually I don't know what I thought I had.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No falls, and his speech is all right day to day. Evenings he gets muddy, though. Mostly people's names.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Family names, or the names of objects too?
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): People. Twice last week he called Daniel, our grandson, by our son's name. Objects are fine — he still makes a cup of tea and finds his glasses.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Daniel. See, I know it. Why the tea? Are you scoring me? What do I have to get right?
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): No score. I'm thinking it through out loud, and I don't have a label for it yet. Are you still driving?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I drive. Since I was seventeen. You're not writing to the DVLA, are you? Is this whole visit about the car?
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not since Tuesday. I took the keys off the hook. He wasn't best pleased.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm banned, is that it? For how many weeks? And what about getting to the chemist if you're at work, Jean?

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not banned, and no letter to the DVLA from me today. I'd like you to stay off the road until this has been looked at, because a short walk that ends at the wrong station matters. Jean can do the chemist run — who sorts the medicines at home?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I do. There's a blue tablet and a white one. Well, actually, she puts them in the little pots, and I don't cough, if the blue one is the cough tablet. Do blood pressure tablets make you cough?

[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I manage all of it. Ramipril five milligrams each morning, for the blood pressure, and atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, for the cholesterol. Both for years. The ramipril is the one that can cause a cough, and he doesn't get one.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good, we'll count the cough as absent then. Anything for the knee?

[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol, one gram, when it's playing up. Not every day — about three times a week. He used to take ibuprofen too, and the chemist stopped that last year when the blood pressure went up.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): So ibuprofen is off, and paracetamol only when he needs it. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. But is the knee arthritis? My neighbour had a new knee and he was in hospital for days. Will you send me for an X-ray?
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No drug allergies that I've ever heard. The hospital said wear and tear, a couple of years ago. They offered an injection, he declined, and we haven't been back.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's osteoarthritis of the knee, already known, and an X-ray today wouldn't change what we do if the pain is stable. Is it worse than your usual, Mr Hale?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Same as ever. Stairs are the worst of it. You said you were thinking out loud — what are you actually thinking? Is it just my age, or is it dementia?

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking of things that can mimic memory trouble, before anyone uses a word like dementia. An underactive thyroid, low B12, a blood count that's off, the kidneys. I am not saying you have dementia — I haven't tested your memory properly enough to say anything of the sort. How are you sleeping?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep. I'm up at six, same as always. Will the blood tests mean I have to starve? And how many needles is it?
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nights are settled. He nods off in the chair after lunch for maybe an hour, but he doesn't wander in the night. Appetite's normal, and his weight hasn't changed.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): No fasting for these, and it's one needle, a few tubes. Weight being steady is helpful. Have you been low, tearful, or not enjoying things, Mr Hale?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not depressed. I'm annoyed, which is different, and I still do the crossword, most of it. Are you going to talk to me, or about me?
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): To you. That's a fair challenge. Jean's already said the appetite and the weight are steady. Any safety worries at home — the cooker, the front door, that sort of thing?
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Last Thursday he left the gas ring on. Only a minute, and I came in and turned it off. Just the once.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): The phone rang. I was going to put the kettle— everyone leaves a ring for a second. It was once. Does that mean I can't be at home on my own, are you going to put me in a home?

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nobody is talking about a home. Once is worth writing down, not a reason to move you. What I want to arrange is bloods today — full blood count, kidney function, thyroid, B12, and cholesterol while we're there, as you're on the statin — and a referral to the memory assessment service. I will not put a diagnosis on you this afternoon.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): A memory assessment. So you do think it's dementia. How many weeks will I wait, and do I have to stay overnight? What if I fail it?

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Failing isn't the way to think of it, and you won't stay overnight. Plenty of people who go are found to have something treatable, or less than the family feared. The wait is often a few weeks, and the clinic will write. I'll see you back here in three weeks for the blood results, even if they haven't reached you by then.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. What if I get worse before that, what should Jean do? And will the needle make me faint, because sometimes I go a bit funny with them?

[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): If there's sudden weakness, a sudden bad headache, or he's much more confused than he is today, don't wait for the three weeks — go to A&E, or ring the surgery the same day. Nurse, can you take the bloods once we're finished?

[SEG0054] person_1 (NURSE): Yes, four tubes, straight after this. Mr Hale, you said you feel faint with needles, so I'll have you lying flat, and your wife can stay. There's no need to fast — breakfast is fine.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): She can stay, good. Is four tubes a lot? Will it bruise? I bruise if they wiggle the needle.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): It can leave a small bruise. I'll go carefully, and you press on the cotton wool for a few minutes afterwards. I'll fetch the bottles.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mrs Hale, keep those keys out of reach for now. Mr Hale, staying off the road stands until we've a clearer picture. Any questions before the bloods?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Only about a hundred, but I'll start with one. If the bloods come back normal, does that mean I'm fine and we cancel the memory place?

[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. Normal bloods would rule a few things out, not the whole question, so the memory assessment still goes ahead. We'll talk it all through again when I see you in three weeks.
